extreme-value-theorem-s1.title: The graph of $f$ on $[-2.5, 4]$
extreme-value-theorem-s1.text: $f(x) = (x + 1)^2 - 2$ for $-2.5 \le x \le 1$ and $f(x) = 2 + (x - 1) - \frac{(x - 1)^2}{2}$ for $1 < x \le 4$. The pieces meet at $(1, 2)$, where the slope jumps from 4 to 1.

plot.label: Graph of f on the closed interval from -2.5 to 4: down to a low point at (-1, -2), up to a corner at (1, 2), on up to a high point at (2, 2.5), then down to (4, 0.5)

extreme-value-theorem-s2.title: The graph of $h$, which jumps at $x = 2$
extreme-value-theorem-s2.text: $h(x) = x$ for $0 \le x < 2$ and $h(x) = x - 3$ for $2 \le x \le 4$.

plot.label: Graph of h on the closed interval from 0 to 4: a line from (0, 0) up to an open circle at (2, 2), then a line from a closed dot at (2, -1) up to (4, 1)

items.q: How many critical points does $f$ have in the open interval $(-2.5, 4)$?

mistakes.why: You found the two flat tangent lines, at $x = -1$ and $x = 2$. A critical point is also an interior point where $f'$ does not exist: the corner at $x = 1$.
The endpoints $x = -2.5$ and $x = 4$ are not critical points: a critical point is an interior point of the domain.

why.correct: $f'(-1) = 0$ and $f'(2) = 0$ (flat tangent lines), and $f'(1)$ does not exist (corner). Three critical points: $x = -1$, $1$, $2$.

items.q: Which statement about $f$ at $x = 1$ is true?
options: $f$ has a relative maximum at $x = 1$, because the graph has a corner there
$x = 1$ is not a critical point, because $f$ is continuous there
$f$ has a relative minimum at $x = 1$, because $f'(1)$ does not exist
$x = 1$ is a critical point, but $f(1)$ is not a relative extremum

why.correct: A critical point is only a candidate. At $x = 1$, $f'$ does not exist, but $f$ is rising on both sides (slopes near 4 on the left, near 1 on the right), so $f(1) = 2$ is neither a relative maximum nor a relative minimum.
options: A corner can be a peak, but this one is not: the graph keeps rising through it.
Continuity does not matter: $f'(1)$ fails to exist, which makes $x = 1$ a critical point.
An undefined derivative makes a critical point, not an extremum. Values just left of 1 are smaller than $f(1)$, values just right are larger.
$f'(1)$ does not exist, so it is a critical point; but $f$ rises on both sides of $x = 1$, so there is no peak or valley.

items.q: What is the absolute minimum value of $f$ on $[-2.5, 4]$?

mistakes.why: $-1$ is where the minimum happens (the $x$-value). The question asks for the value, $f(-1)$.
$f(4) = 0.5$ is the lowest value on the right, but the graph goes lower at $x = -1$.

why.correct: The lowest point of the graph is $(-1, -2)$, lower than both endpoint values $f(-2.5) = 0.25$ and $f(4) = 0.5$. The absolute minimum value is $-2$.

items.q: At which values of $x$ does $f$ have a relative extremum? Select each one.

why.correct: Relative minimum at $x = -1$ (value $-2$) and relative maximum at $x = 2$ (value $2.5$). The corner at $x = 1$ is a critical point without an extremum.
options: A valley: $f$ falls, then rises. Relative minimum.
The graph rises through the corner; no peak or valley.
A peak: $f$ rises, then falls. Relative maximum.
At $x = 3$ the graph is falling; nothing special happens.

items.q: What is the absolute maximum of $f$ on $[-2.5, 4]$, and where does it occur?
options: $2$, at the corner $x = 1$
$0.5$, at the right endpoint $x = 4$
No maximum exists, since $f$ is not differentiable at $x = 1$

why.correct: $f$ is continuous on $[-2.5, 4]$, so the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees an absolute maximum. It is $f(2) = 2.5$, the highest point of the graph.
options: $(2, 2.5)$ is the highest point of the whole graph, above both endpoint values.
$f(1) = 2$ is less than $f(2) = 2.5$.
An endpoint can hold the maximum, but $f(4) = 0.5$ is not the largest value.
The Extreme Value Theorem needs continuity, not differentiability. $f$ is continuous on the closed interval.

items.q: Does the Extreme Value Theorem guarantee that $h$ has an absolute maximum on $[0, 4]$?
options: Yes, because $[0, 4]$ is a closed interval
Yes, because $h$ is defined at each point of $[0, 4]$
No, because $h$ is not differentiable at $x = 0$
No, because $h$ is not continuous at $x = 2$

why.correct: The Extreme Value Theorem needs $h$ continuous on $[0, 4]$. $h$ jumps at $x = 2$ ($\lim_{x \to 2^-} h(x) = 2$ but $h(2) = -1$), so the theorem guarantees nothing.
options: A closed interval is half the hypothesis; $h$ must also be continuous on it.
Defined is not enough: $h$ jumps from values near 2 down to $-1$.
Differentiability is not a hypothesis of the Extreme Value Theorem, and $x = 0$ is an endpoint.
The theorem needs continuity on the closed interval; the jump at 2 breaks it.

items.q: Which statement about $h$ on $[0, 4]$ is true?
options: $h$ has neither, because the Extreme Value Theorem does not apply
$h$ has an absolute maximum of $2$, at $x = 2$
$h$ has an absolute minimum, $-1$, but no absolute maximum
$h$ has an absolute maximum of $1$, at the endpoint $x = 4$

why.correct: The lowest value is $h(2) = -1$. For a maximum, $h(x) = x$ gets as close to 2 as you like as $x \to 2^-$ but never equals 2, and no value is larger, so there is no absolute maximum.
options: When a hypothesis fails, the theorem promises nothing; extrema may still exist. Here the minimum does.
$h(2) = -1$, not 2: the open circle at $(2, 2)$ is not on the graph.
$h(2) = -1$ is the lowest value. Values near $x = 2$ from the left get close to 2 but never reach it, and every value of $h$ is less than 2.
$h(1.5) = 1.5$ is larger than $h(4) = 1$, so 1 is not the largest value.

items.q: What does the Extreme Value Theorem say about $h$ on $[2, 4]$?
options: Nothing, because $h$ jumps at $x = 2$
$h$ is continuous there, so it has both: maximum $1$, minimum $-1$
$h$ has an absolute maximum there but perhaps no absolute minimum
$h$ has a critical point in $(2, 4)$ where its extremes occur

why.correct: On $[2, 4]$, $h(x) = x - 3$ is continuous (including $h(2) = -1$). The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees both extremes: minimum $h(2) = -1$, maximum $h(4) = 1$.
options: The jump is approached from the left of 2, outside $[2, 4]$. On $[2, 4]$ itself $h$ is continuous.
On $[2, 4]$, $h(x) = x - 3$ with $h(2) = -1$: no jump inside or at the ends of this interval.
The theorem gives both: an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum.
$h'(x) = 1$ on $(2, 4)$; there are no critical points. The extremes are at the endpoints.

items.q: What is the absolute maximum value of $h$ on $[0, 1.5]$?

mistakes.why: 2 is the height of the open circle at $x = 2$, outside $[0, 1.5]$. On this interval the highest point is at the right endpoint.

why.correct: On $[0, 1.5]$, $h(x) = x$ is continuous and rising, so the maximum is at the endpoint: $h(1.5) = 1.5$.

items.q: Which are critical points of $f(x) = x^3 - 12x + 1$? Select each one.
Where does $f(x) = (x - 3)^{2/3}$ have a critical point?
options: At $x = 0$, where $f'(x) = 0$
At $x = 3$, where $f'(x) = 0$
At $x = 3$, where $f'$ does not exist
No critical point, since $f'(x) = 0$ has no solution

why.correct: $f'(x) = \frac{2}{3\sqrt[3]{x - 3}}$ is never 0 and is undefined at $x = 3$, which is in the domain of $f$. So $x = 3$ is the one critical point (a cusp).
options: $f'(3)$ is undefined, not zero: the graph has a cusp.
$f'(x) = \frac{2}{3}(x - 3)^{-1/3}$ is undefined at $x = 3$, an interior point of the domain.
A critical point is also a point where $f'$ does not exist.

items.q: Find the critical point of $f(x) = x e^{-x}$.

mistakes.why: You kept only $x \cdot (-e^{-x})$. The product rule has two terms: $f'(x) = e^{-x} - x e^{-x} = (1 - x)e^{-x}$.
Check the chain rule: the derivative of $e^{-x}$ is $-e^{-x}$, so $f'(x) = (1 - x)e^{-x}$, zero at $x = 1$.

why.correct: $f'(x) = e^{-x} + x(-e^{-x}) = (1 - x)e^{-x}$. Since $e^{-x} > 0$, $f'(x) = 0$ only at $x = 1$, and $f'$ exists everywhere.

items.q: Find the critical points of $f(x) = x - 2\sin x$ on $(0, 2\pi)$.
options: $x = \frac{\pi}{3}$ and $x = \frac{5\pi}{3}$
$x = \frac{\pi}{6}$ and $x = \frac{5\pi}{6}$
$x = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $x = \frac{4\pi}{3}$
$x = \pi$ alone
$\cos x = \frac{1}{2}$ at these two angles in $(0, 2\pi)$.
These solve $\sin x = \frac{1}{2}$. The derivative of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$.
These solve $\cos x = -\frac{1}{2}$: check the sign of $f'(x) = 1 - 2\cos x$.

items.q: Find the critical point of $f(x) = \frac{\ln x}{x}$ for $x > 0$. Give an exact answer.

mistakes.why: At $x = 1$, $\ln x = 0$, so $f(1) = 0$; but the question is where $f'(x) = \frac{1 - \ln x}{x^2}$ is zero.
$x = 0$ is not in the domain of $f$, so it cannot be a critical point.

why.correct: Quotient rule: $f'(x) = \frac{x \cdot \frac{1}{x} - \ln x}{x^2} = \frac{1 - \ln x}{x^2}$. It is zero when $\ln x = 1$, so $x = e$.

items.q: $f$ is continuous on $[1, 5]$. Which statement earns credit for "$f$ has an absolute maximum on $[1, 5]$"?
options: "$f$ has a critical point, so $f$ has an absolute maximum there."
"By the Mean Value Theorem, $f'(c) = 0$ for some $c$, so $f$ has an absolute maximum."
"$f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[1, 5]$, so by the Extreme Value Theorem $f$ has an absolute maximum there."
"$f$ has an absolute maximum because a function on a closed interval has one."

why.correct: The Extreme Value Theorem: if $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then $f$ has at least one absolute maximum value and one absolute minimum value on $[a, b]$.
options: A critical point is a candidate, not a guarantee of anything.
The Mean Value Theorem is about slopes and needs $f(1) = f(5)$ to give $f'(c) = 0$; it does not give extrema.
It names the theorem and its hypothesis: continuous on a closed interval.
False: a function with a jump may have no maximum. Continuity is required.

items.q: For $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ on $[0, 4]$, which statement is true?
options: $x = 0$ is a critical point, because $f'(0)$ does not exist
$f$ has no critical points in $(0, 4)$; its absolute minimum is at the endpoint $x = 0$
$f$ has no absolute minimum, because it has no critical points
The absolute maximum is at a critical point inside $(0, 4)$

why.correct: On $(0, 4)$, $f'(x) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$ exists and is positive, so there are no critical points. Absolute extremes then occur at the endpoints: minimum $f(0) = 0$, maximum $f(4) = 2$.
options: A critical point must be an interior point of the domain; $x = 0$ is an endpoint.
$f'(x) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} > 0$ on $(0, 4)$. The extremes are at the ends: $f(0) = 0$, $f(4) = 2$.
The Extreme Value Theorem still applies (continuous on $[0, 4]$); the extremes sit at endpoints.
There is no critical point inside. The maximum, $2$, is at the endpoint $x = 4$.

items.q: For $f(x) = x^2$ on the open interval $(-1, 2)$, which statement is true?
options: $f$ has an absolute minimum of 0 but no absolute maximum
$f$ has an absolute maximum of 4 at $x = 2$
$f$ has both, by the Extreme Value Theorem
$f$ has an absolute maximum of 1, reached at the endpoint $x = -1$

why.correct: On an open interval the Extreme Value Theorem does not apply. Here the minimum $f(0) = 0$ exists, but $x^2$ gets close to 4 without reaching it, so there is no absolute maximum.
options: $f(0) = 0$ is the smallest value. Values near $x = 2$ approach 4, but $x = 2$ is not in the interval.
$x = 2$ is excluded from an open interval.
The theorem needs a closed interval.
$x = -1$ is excluded, and values near $x = 2$ are bigger than 1 anyway.

items.q: For $f(x) = x^3$, $f'(0) = 0$. What kind of point is $x = 0$?
options: A relative minimum, because $f'(0) = 0$
A relative maximum, because the tangent line is flat
Not a critical point, because $f(0) = 0$
A critical point that is not a relative extremum

why.correct: $f'(x) = 3x^2$ is 0 at $x = 0$, so it is a critical point. But $f(x) < 0$ just left of 0 and $f(x) > 0$ just right of it, so $f(0)$ is neither a relative maximum nor a relative minimum.
options: $f'(0) = 0$ makes 0 a candidate only. Negative values just left of 0 are smaller than $f(0)$.
A flat tangent line can sit on a rising graph, as here.
The value of $f$ does not matter; $f'(0) = 0$ makes it a critical point.
$x^3 < 0$ to the left of 0 and $x^3 > 0$ to the right, so there is no peak or valley.
